learning_objective: 🎯 Discover the 'helper verbs' that change the mood of a sentence, and learn how to politely ask for permission or give strong advice!

key_vocabulary.hindi_meaning: भावसूचक क्रिया (मन का भाव बताने वाली)

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Auxiliary verbs are 'helping verbs' that team up with main verbs to show tense or make questions. The Big Three are BE (is, am, are, was, were), DO (do, does, did), and HAVE (has, have, had). Example: 'She IS running.' 'Is' helps 'running' make sense!

Modals are special helper verbs that show the 'mood' or attitude of the speaker. They tell us if something is possible, allowed, or necessary. Words like Can, Could, May, Might, Should, and Must are modals. They NEVER change their spelling!

'Can' shows ability (I CAN lift this box = I have the strength). 'May' asks for formal permission. If you ask a teacher, 'CAN I go to the washroom?', you are asking if you have the physical ability to walk there. You should ask 'MAY I go to the washroom?' to get permission!

'Should' is used to give friendly advice. Example: 'You SHOULD drink water.' (It is a good idea). 'Must' is a strict rule or obligation. Example: 'You MUST wear a helmet on a bike.' (You have no choice, it is the law!).

Both show that something is possible. Use 'May' when there is a good 50-50 chance. Example: 'It MAY rain today' (look at those dark clouds). Use 'Might' when the chance is very low. Example: 'I MIGHT win the lottery' (probably not, but who knows!).

fun_activity.title: 🕵️‍♂️ The Rule Maker Game
fun_activity.instructions: Pretend you are the Principal of your school for a day. Write down 3 strict rules using 'MUST' and 3 pieces of friendly advice for students using 'SHOULD'.

quick_recap: ⭐ Auxiliaries (is, do, have) help main verbs show tense.
⭐ Modals (can, must, should) show ability, permission, or obligation.
⭐ Modals never change spelling (no 's' or 'ing' forms) and are always followed by a base verb.
⭐ Use 'May' for formal permission and 'Can' for physical ability.
⭐ Use 'Should' for advice and 'Must' for strict rules.
